paras: The beating of Henry Proctor was an attack on a 16-year-old Black high-school student by six white boys armed with sticks at Forty-third Street and Forrestville Avenue on the South Side of Chicago, Illinois, around the end of April 1919. The Chicago Broad Ax reported it as "further evidence of racial bitterness on the south side" under a headline presenting it as part of a continuing "race war."
Proctor lived at 4333 Forrestville Avenue, near the corner where he was attacked, and was a pupil at Wendell Phillips High School.

According to what his mother told the police, Proctor met the six boys at Forty-third Street and Forrestville Avenue "the first of this week," that is, early in the week before the paper's Saturday, May 3, issue. As he tried to go past them, one of the boys reportedly said, "You're the guy who insulted my sister," and the group beat him with sticks. The report does not describe the extent of his injuries.

Mrs. Proctor notified the police, telling them her son had been beaten "because he was colored" and that he knew no white girls. No report of arrests or of any further police action was found in the coverage.

The only located account appeared on page 5 of the Chicago Broad Ax on May 3, 1919, under the headline "Colored Boy Is Beaten as Race War Continues." The short item set the attack within a wider pattern of racial hostility on the South Side, called the beating a "slugging," and relayed the attackers' claim of an insult only alongside the mother's denial. No account in the Chicago Defender was found.

The reason for the attack rests on two versions in the same report: the boys' claim that Proctor had insulted one of their sisters, relayed through the police, and his mother's statement that he knew no white girls and was attacked because he was Black.
